pages.text: A thin man stands at your gate with a ledger under his arm. He does not smile, and he does not look unkind either. He looks like someone who counts. “Master Quill,” he says. “The Lord's steward.”
“The old farm smokes again,” he says, and looks at your chimney. “The Lord wishes to know why.” You tell him: because somebody lives here. He writes that down.
Quill counts everything. Cows, sacks, windows, nails. He counts the hens twice, because one moved. Every number goes into his ledger, written with a very sharp pencil.
Later you find two ledger pages folded into a paper boat on the pond. Somewhere, a very small bell tinkles. Quill is not amused. You are, a little.
Under the stones of the old glasshouse you find a rusty tin. Inside is a yellow paper, folded in three: the lease. It says the farm shall give the Lord “… a half of all that the land gives.” A half.

You take out the burnt page you have kept since your first day. Circled twice at the bottom: “one in two.” The same number. You put the lease in a drawer and shut it. You know it is there, which is nearly as bad.

Quill is at the gate again. “The Lord's share,” he says. “And the north field.” Your north field is resting, green and buzzing and full of bees. “The Book,” says Quill, “has no line for a field that grows nothing.”

“Oh, pay it!” says Lark, swinging his legs on the fence. “Plough it up! Drain the pond! Cut down the forest, it's only standing there!” “No,” you say. It comes out before you know it. “That's what they did, and the ground went thin.”

“The north field rests this year,” you tell Quill. Your voice is smaller than you hoped. But it does not shake. “Have you counted the clover?” Lark asks him, kindly. “It's been counting you.” Quill writes that down too. Lark is gone.
You step into the new room for your books, and stop. Somebody has sorted them all by weight. The heaviest is at the bottom, the lightest at the top, in a perfect slope.

Lark sits on the heaviest, reading a pamphlet about turnips. “Very good system. The heavy ones hold up the others.” “How did you get in?” “Door,” says Lark. “A sort of wall that opens.” The chair is empty. You leave the books as they are.

c4_pizza.title: Pizza night
c4_pizza.text: On the village square the builders eat pizza at long tables under paper lanterns. You sit between Bo and Greenstem. Someone passes you the biggest slice. Tonight, nobody asks whose family you are.

pages.text: A pony stands at your gate and poses, one hoof forward. Then she lets you load a sack, a crate and a big order for the village. She walks down the road as if she owns it.

On the square, people stop. They look at the pony, then the order, then you. Somebody says your name. Your own name, not your family's. The fourth line comes back: “Strong pony brings the world its bread.”

Quill asks, because the Book says he must, to borrow your pony and cart for the Lord's road. The pony turns her head and shows him her other profile. Quill looks at her for a long time. He writes “declined (pony)” and underlines it twice.

At the end of the season Quill rides back up to the Hurst with his ledger full. At the gate he looks back. “The farm gives back more than it takes,” he says, as if it were a question. “The Lord will want to know.”
“Was the Lord a villain?” asks Minena. You think about it for a long time. “He was afraid,” you say. “That's worse, sometimes.”
Nobody says anything. Then the smallest one whispers, “Afraid of what?” “Of a number,” you say. “Now go to sleep.” They do not. Not yet.
